title: Past nearby detections had a stronger link than future detections to Finnish moth reappearance in 1998-2021
abstract: We tested annual nearby detection supply as a marker of Finnish moth reappearance after two zero years. We used released species records and European thermal scores, not BBS or network summaries. The sample had 320,598 species-site-year records, 18,716 reappearances, 655 species and 61 traps in 1998-2021. Models included species-site, species-year and site-year fixed effects. In a joint past-future model, a 0.10 increase in past supply had a 1.66 percentage point association with reappearance (95% interval 1.25-2.06); future supply had a 1.21 point association (0.84-1.57). The past-minus-future difference was 0.45 points (0.03-0.87), with three-way cluster uncertainty and an allowance for many fixed effects. Persistent detections and matched donor coverage kept positive associations. The large future association limits a causal source interpretation. Source-linked reappearance can occur in a moth network whose broader community change was near its spatial warming benchmark. These results do not identify dispersal limitation or its share of the thermal gap. Detection, habitat, weather, selected records and dynamic-panel bias remain limits. The package gives code, aggregate evidence, input hashes and reproduction instructions.

display.caption: Left: unadjusted reappearance rates by past source group; tied quantiles give four groups. Right: joint past and future source slopes, with three-way cluster intervals and a conservative fixed-effect degrees-of-freedom allowance. Future associations limit causal interpretation.
